extracted.intended_audience: general public, journalists, researchers and policymakers interested in misinformation and media literacy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and taxonomies for defining, identifying, classifying, and responding to 'fake news' and related information disorders, aimed at readers seeking to recognise false or misleading news and choose mitigation strategies. Covers identification checklists, types of problematic content, detection methods, individual and platform-level countermeasures, and legal/regulatory approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: fake news
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news is false or misleading information presented as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term covers misinformation, disinformation, propaganda and hoaxes presented with the aesthetics/legitimacy of news; aims include damaging reputations or making money via advertising. The term is broad and contested; researchers often prefer 'information disorder' as a neutral umbrella.

rubrics_metrics.name: IFLA: Consider the source
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the source to understand its mission and purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the publisher's mission and potential incentives (financial, political). Reliable outlets and known institutions are more likely to adhere to journalistic standards; obscure sources may impersonate reputable outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: IFLA: Read beyond the headline
rubrics_metrics.description: Read beyond the headline to understand the whole story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headlines can be misleading or sensational. Verify claims in the body text and look for supporting evidence before sharing or acting on a headline.

rubrics_metrics.name: IFLA: Check the authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Check the authors to see if they are real and credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify author identity, qualifications, and track record. Look for author pages, institutional affiliations, or previous credible work; absence or fabrication of author details is a red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: IFLA: Assess the supporting sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the supporting sources to ensure they support the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow links and citations to primary sources; check if sources are accurately represented and whether they are independent, authoritative, and recent.

rubrics_metrics.name: IFLA: Check the date of publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Check the date of publication to see if the story is relevant and up to date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Old content can be recirculated as new and misleading; ensure chronological context is accurate before drawing conclusions or sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: IFLA: Ask if it is a joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask if it is meant to be satire or parody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some sites intentionally publish satirical content; check site disclaimers and tone. Satire may include non-factual elements intended to amuse rather than deceive.

rubrics_metrics.name: IFLA: Review your own biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Review your own biases to see if they are affecting your judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of confirmation bias and motivated reasoning; question whether you are more likely to accept or share content that aligns with pre-existing beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: IFLA: Ask experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask experts to get confirmation from independent people with knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult independent subject-matter experts or reputable fact-checkers when claims are technical, specialized, or consequential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wardle taxonomy: satire or parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire or parody — no intention to cause harm but has potential to fool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical pieces may be mistaken for real reporting; check for signals (site design, disclaimers, absurdity) and consider context to avoid misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wardle taxonomy: false connection
rubrics_metrics.description: False connection — when headlines, visuals or captions don't support the content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mismatch between headline/visuals and article text is a common attention-grabbing tactic; verify whether the lead elements accurately reflect the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wardle taxonomy: misleading content
rubrics_metrics.description: Misleading content — misleading use of information to frame an issue or an individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content may selectively present facts, omit context, or use framing to distort interpretation; check fuller context and original sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wardle taxonomy: false context
rubrics_metrics.description: False context — genuine content shared with false contextual information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify when and where an image/video/text was originally produced; repurposed content can mislead by implying a different event or timeframe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wardle taxonomy: impostor content
rubrics_metrics.description: Impostor content — when genuine sources are impersonated with false, made-up sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for subtle site or URL differences, forged bylines, or cloned designs; verify via publisher contact pages and authoritative archives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wardle taxonomy: manipulated content
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulated content — genuine information or imagery manipulated to deceive (e.g., doctored photo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reverse image searches, metadata checks, and visual forensics to detect edits; manipulated images/videos are central to many hoaxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wardle taxonomy: fabricated content
rubrics_metrics.description: Fabricated content — new content that is 100% false, designed to deceive and do harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completely invented stories with no factual basis are often designed for political or financial gain; check for independent corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific denialism as a type
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific denialism — producing false or misleading facts to unconsciously support strong pre-existing beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often appears in health, environment and science contexts; evaluate claims against scientific consensus and peer-reviewed evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information disorder categories: misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Misinformation — false information disseminated without harmful intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mistakes, misunderstandings, or misinterpretations spread by people who do not intend to deceive; responses emphasise correction and education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information disorder categories: disinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Disinformation — false information created and shared by people with harmful intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate falsehoods intended to deceive, polarize, or manipulate; often coordinated and may involve hostile state or organisational actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information disorder categories: malinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Malinformation — sharing of genuine information with the intent to cause harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True facts used maliciously via selective release, doxxing, or outing; responses may involve legal, ethical, and platform moderation considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic and affective cues for identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news language tends to be more inflammatory and 'clickbait' with eye-catching titles intended to confuse and generate clicks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for excessive emotion, sensationalist wording, and claims lacking precise sourcing. Researchers use linguistic features (e.g., n-grams, bag-of-words) as signals in automated models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual cues and image verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual-based cues help assess if a picture or video was legitimate or doctored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reverse image search, check metadata, and apply forensic techniques to detect manipulation; mismatched images (false context) are common in viral falsehoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social-context and propagation features
rubrics_metrics.description: Social context features (who shares it, network propagation, super-spreaders) matter for categorizing and predicting fake news spread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine sharing patterns, influential accounts, coordinated networks, and virality metrics; super-spreaders can amplify false stories rapidly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated detection and modelling techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated methods (machine learning, NLP, network analysis) can help detect fake news using linguistic, visual and social features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models employ n-gram encodings, bag-of-words, and network features; limitations include training set bias, evolving misinformation tactics, and risks of false positives.

rubrics_metrics.name: IFCN / fact-checking standards and practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact-checking organisations adhere to codes of principles and verification practices (e.g., training, vetting, blind peer review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent fact-checkers provide extra checks, transparency, and editorial oversight; however professional fact-checking is resource-intensive and not fully scalable to all claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique rebuttal — expose faulty reasoning (cherry-picking, fake experts) rather than solely supplying contrasting facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build trust through respectful exchange, ask what evidence would change minds, and illustrate logical fallacies; may be more effective than fact-only corrections for some audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of facts over emotions / information flooding
rubrics_metrics.description: Counter emotional misinformation by flooding information spaces with factual news and emphasizing evidence-based reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase visibility of high-quality journalism and factual content on platforms to drown out misinformation; requires sustained editorial and platform commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual counteraction and caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals should confront misinformation when spotted but exercise caution: debunking low-impact falsehoods can unintentionally amplify them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, evidence-based replies may help; avoid giving undue attention to obscure false claims that could gain traction when debunked in high-profile outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backfire effect caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrective information can sometimes reinforce mistaken beliefs among strongly committed audiences (backfire effect), though more recent evidence suggests it's uncommon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of elite cues and social identity influences; tailor corrective strategies (technique rebuttal, trusted messengers) rather than assuming factual correction will always work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform regulation and self-regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation/self-regulation of social media and search engines to reduce incentives and reach of fake news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include legally enforced measures, platform policies, transparency obligations, and changes to algorithms that currently prioritise engagement; tradeoffs include freedom of expression and risk of overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform countermeasures: down-ranking and warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Tech companies use two main counter-strategies: down-ranking problematic content and attaching warning labels/messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Down-ranking reduces visibility but risks false positives; warnings reduce sharing and misperceptions but require timely fact-checks and are less effective for biased coverage that is partially true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasise reliable sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Place greater emphasis on reliable sources (e.g., Wikipedia, mainstream media, science communicators) during breaking news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promoting authoritative coverage can help, but results are mixed because hyperpartisan content and confirmation bias can exist even in mainstream outlets; some audiences may reject scientific commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban or limit super-spreaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Target or ban super-spreaders of fake news on social media to reduce large-scale amplification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing highly influential repeat offenders can curb spread, but raises questions about enforcement criteria and potential political bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checking scalability limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional fact-checking is slow and resource-intensive; many false claims never get checked during peak viral spread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of scale and speed, fact-checking must be complemented with automated signals, platform interventions, prebunking, and media literacy efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nudges and reflection prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use nudges (e.g., 'read before you retweet') to prompt reflection and reduce unreflective sharing of false information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple UX nudges can improve accuracy judgments and reduce impulsive sharing; Twitter-style prompts are an example of technology-based nudges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media literacy and critical thinking education
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach critical media literacy skills so readers can self-evaluate the accuracy of content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed critical thinking and verification practices in school and university curricula; media literacy helps readers check sources, evaluate claims, and resist manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inoculation theory / prebunking / mental immunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Prebunking (inoculation) exposes people to weakened forms of false arguments or explains deceptive techniques to build resistance before encountering misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include listing common myths and deconstructing the flaws, using parallel argumentation and humour; prebunking has been shown promising in countering denialism and recurring false narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and criminal sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some countries enact laws criminalising 'fake news' or misinformation deemed harmful to public order or state security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Algeria, Turkey, Iran and others; criminalisation raises freedom of expression and human rights concerns and can be used to suppress dissent or independent journalism.
